source: Emery & Clayton (2001) Effects of experience and social context on prospective caching strategies by scrub jays, Nature 414:443
finding: Western scrub jays that had been watched while caching later re-cached food in new sites. Jays caching in private did not. Reading: jays act to cut theft risk when a possible thief saw them.
numbers: Observer+pilferer group, n=7. Davis: proportion re-cached 0.44 observed vs 0.06 private (Z=2.20, P<0.05). Cambridge replication with the same birds: 0.28 vs 0.08 (Z=2.20, P<0.05). When observed, re-caching went mostly to new sites (n=7, Z=2.20, P<0.05); in private, no old/new preference.
limits: Tiny n=7 with Wilcoxon tests. Same birds at both sites, so the Cambridge replication is not independent. Species corrected to A. californica in a 2002 erratum.
agent_relevance: Behaviour is keyed to context: protect information when a possible thief was present. A trigger (observer seen) changes the action; it is not a fixed routine.

source: Emery & Clayton (2001) Effects of experience and social context on prospective caching strategies by scrub jays, Nature 414:443, interleaved trays
finding: Birds tracked the social context of each separate caching episode. With two trays cached minutes apart, they re-cached more from the tray cached while watched.
numbers: Observed tray vs private tray, n=7: proportion re-cached 0.45 vs 0.04 (Z=2.37, P<0.05); proportion recovered 0.73 vs 0.39 (Z=2.37, P<0.05); number cached the same (3.93 vs 3.57).
limits: Rules out a general 'I was watched today' tendency. Cannot separate 'remembers who saw' from 'remembers the context was watched'.
agent_relevance: Tag each item with who saw it and when, not one global flag.

source: Emery & Clayton (2001) Effects of experience and social context on prospective caching strategies by scrub jays, Nature 414:443, experience effect
finding: Only jays that had themselves pilfered others' caches re-cached selectively when watched. Observer-only jays did not.
numbers: Observer+pilferer and pilferer groups: more re-caching in new sites when observed (each n=7, Z=2.20 to 2.37, P<0.05). Observer-only group: no selective re-caching (old sites Z=1.6, P>0.1).
limits: Fits experience projection (the bird uses its own thief experience). Alternative: thieving taught a learned rule about observers. Not separated here.
agent_relevance: Competence at modelling a rival may need having played the rival's role.

source: Bugnyar & Heinrich (2005) Ravens, Corvus corax, differentiate between knowledgeable and ignorant competitors, Proc R Soc B
finding: Ravens changed cache-protection and pilfer tactics depending on whether a competitor had watched the caching or had its view blocked by opaque curtains.
numbers: Exp 1 (7 hand-raised ravens, n=6 analysed): storers recovered more caches near former observers than non-observers (T=0, p=0.032), only when observers moved toward the caches. Observers found more caches than non-observers in private (p=0.032) but not with the storer present (T=3, p=0.16).
limits: Seven birds; exact Wilcoxon with n=6 has a floor of p=0.032. Authors say approach-pattern cues and own memory of who was present are not fully excluded.
agent_relevance: Selective protection tied to the other's information state, tested against simple behaviour cues. Lesson: run the discriminating control, not only the headline.
quote: ravens not only recall whom they had seen during caching, but also know that obstacles can obstruct the view of others

source: Bugnyar & Heinrich (2005) experiment 2
finding: As pilferers, ravens delayed pilfering when the dominant competitor was ignorant, and went straight to the cache when the dominant had also watched the caching.
numbers: Time to pilfer about 10x longer with a dominant non-observer than a dominant co-observer (n=6, T=0, p=0.032). Mean distance to competitor 6 m vs 0.6 m. Subordinate pilfer success 69% with non-observers vs 12% with co-observers. Overall chi2(4)=11.35, p=0.023.
limits: Same small group. Authors say showing awareness of blocked sight does not prove human-like mental-state understanding.
agent_relevance: Strategy shifts with what the rival can infer and with payoff. A model of the other must drive the action rule, not only the description.

source: Bugnyar, Reber & Buckner (2016) Ravens attribute visual access to unseen competitors, Nat Commun 7:10506
finding: Ravens guarded caches when they heard conspecifics and a peephole was open, but not when it was closed. No gaze cue was available, so a gaze-based behaviour rule cannot explain it.
numbers: 10 ravens (9 in the peephole condition). Time to finish a cache: peephole faster than non-observed (n=9, Z=-2.666, P=0.012 Bonferroni); revisits to improve: fewer (Z=2.539, P=0.024). Peephole vs observed: P=0.08 and P=0.94 (no difference). Omnibus chi2=14.889 and 12.929, both P<0.001.
limits: Ravens did not reliably cache away from the open peephole (1.78 caches in view vs 2.78 out of view, P=0.297), a limit on the attribution. Authors accept it shows seeing-attribution, not belief.
agent_relevance: Experience projection: generalising from own perception to others. A test that removes the surface cue so only inference can pass.

source: Hare, Call, Agnetta & Tomasello (2000) Chimpanzees know what conspecifics do and do not see, Anim Behav 59:771
finding: Subordinate chimpanzees competing with dominants took food the dominant could not see far more than food both could see. (Abstract-level, from search summary; text not opened.)
numbers: Dominants got virtually all foods both could see; subordinates were often successful in three situations where they had better visual access. Exact counts not read.
limits: Not opened. A search summary says Povinelli et al. 1994 and Call et al. 2000 did not replicate with other procedures.
agent_relevance: Competition gives a stronger signal than cooperation because the animal is motivated; a task design lesson.

source: Hare, Call & Tomasello (2001) Do chimpanzees know what conspecifics know? Anim Behav 61:139
finding: Follow-up: tested whether subordinates were sensitive to what the dominant had or had not seen during baiting, not only what it can see now. (Search summary only.)
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Knowledge (what was seen earlier) versus momentary seeing is the key split.

source: Krupenye, Kano, Hirata, Call & Tomasello (2016) Great apes anticipate that other individuals will act according to false beliefs, Science 354:110
finding: Eye tracking: apes looked first to the place where an actor falsely believed an object was, though the apes knew it was gone. Authors read this as implicit false-belief understanding.
numbers: Exp 1 N=40 (19 chimps, 14 bonobos, 7 orangutans): of 30 who looked, 20 looked first at the target, P=0.098 binomial (not significant alone). Exp 2 N=30: 17 of 22, P=0.016. Combined N=29: Z=3.25, P=0.001, r=0.42.
limits: 10 of 40 and 8 of 30 apes made no look. Exp 1 alone not significant. One test trial per subject per experiment. Authors admit the rule 'agents search where they last saw things' still fits. Two earlier gaze studies failed with monkeys.
agent_relevance: The strongest claim for belief tracking in non-humans is implicit and small. A 'last-seen' rule may be enough; do not build belief models beyond need.
quote: Apes did not simply expect the actor's ignorance to lead to error or uncertainty

source: Krupenye et al. (2017) A test of the submentalizing hypothesis: apes' performance in a false belief task inanimate control, Commun Integr Biol
finding: Control suggested by Heyes: actor replaced by a green semi-circle and King Kong by a triangle. Apes made fewer anticipatory looks and showed no bias to the target.
numbers: N=43 apes. Only 22 of 43 (51.16%) looked at a box vs 22 of 30 (73.33%) originally. First looks: 14 of 22 to target, p=0.28. FB1 6 of 11 (p=1.0), FB2 8 of 11 (p=0.23). Viewing time F(1,37)=0.31, p=0.57, eta2=0.008.
limits: 14 of 22 is close to 17 of 22 in size, so the control differs mainly in look rate and power. A null is not proof of mentalizing. Authors found no evidence for submentalizing.
agent_relevance: Matched inanimate controls separate social inference from low-level cueing. Use them for agent tests.

source: Martin & Santos (2014) Monkeys represent others' knowledge but not their beliefs, Dev Sci
finding: Rhesus macaques, infant-style looking-time task: they expect an agent with true knowledge to search correctly, but make no prediction for an agent with a false belief.
numbers: Exp 1: looked longer when the presenter reached into the empty box, 4.34 s vs 3.04 s, t(60)=2.10, p=.04. Familiarisation looking no different (3.70 vs 4.55 s, p=.15). Three studies; the false-belief one showed no difference.
limits: Free-ranging monkeys, between-subjects looking time. Such measures have replication problems in human infants.
agent_relevance: Knowledge tracking and belief tracking can dissociate. A 'who saw it' tag covers many cases; false-belief tracking is a costly extra.

source: Horschler, MacLean & Santos (2020) Do non-human primates really represent others' beliefs? Trends Cogn Sci 24:594
finding: Review urging caution: anticipatory-looking evidence for primate belief faces the same replication, method and theory problems as the human infant literature. (Search summary only.)
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened. Notes most such studies come from a handful of labs; asks for multi-lab replication.
agent_relevance: Evidence resting on one measure from one lab family should be down-weighted.

source: Horschler, MacLean & Santos (2019) Do non-human primates really represent others' ignorance? A test of the awareness relations hypothesis, Cognition
finding: Macaques expected an agent to know a fruit's location after the box moved while the agent could not see, but not after the fruit itself briefly moved. Fits an awareness-relations heuristic.
numbers: Exp 1 box-moves: incorrect reach 3.19 s vs correct 2.32 s (n=36 each; t(69.86)=2.05, p=.04, d=.48). Exp 2 replication: 3.65 s vs 2.36 s (n=50 each; t(96.89)=3.95, p<.001, d=.79).
limits: Large attrition (for example 61 failed to watch, 64 left). Free-ranging looking time.
agent_relevance: Heuristic account: the agent is 'aware of' what it saw, and the link breaks if the object is arbitrarily changed unseen. Like a simple provenance rule.

source: Horschler et al. (2021) How do non-human primates represent others' awareness of where objects are hidden? (PMC8154671)
finding: Macaques expect knowledgeable agents to search correctly after a colour change but not after an unseen size/shape change. Supports heuristic accounts.
numbers: Abstract-level: looked longer at incorrect search after the colour (non-geometric) change, not after the size/shape (geometric) change. Exp 3 confirmed monkeys could detect the colour change.
limits: Only the abstract section was read. Free-ranging looking time.
agent_relevance: Rule-based awareness tracking that breaks in predictable ways: a template for perturbation tests of LLM belief tracking.

source: Chimpanzees gesture to humans in mirrors: using reflection to dissociate seeing from line of gaze (2018, Anim Behav; PMC5877477)
finding: Chimpanzees gestured more when an experimenter could see them through a mirror even without a direct line of gaze. Read as experience projection from their own mirror use.
numbers: Abstract-level: significantly more visual gestures when the experimenter could see them (via mirror) than when not, even with head turned away.
limits: Only the abstract section was read. Authors discuss low-level alternatives.
agent_relevance: Same logic as the raven peephole study: remove the usual cue and keep the inference.

source: Heyes (2015) Animal mindreading: what's the problem? Psychon Bull Rev 22:313
finding: The field lacks agreed alternatives to full mindreading and tests to separate them. Proposes inanimate controls, species unlikely to mindread, and a 'goggles method' (give subjects experience with a new object, then test their use of it on others).
numbers: No data. A 16-page theoretical review citing Penn & Povinelli 2007 and Call & Tomasello 2008.
limits: Theory paper. Associative-learning alternatives are hard to falsify, as critics note.
agent_relevance: Gives the control logic for any 'does the agent model others?' test, including LLMs: matched non-social controls and novel cues.
quote: after some 35 years of research on mindreading in animals, there is still nothing resembling a consensus

source: Kosinski (2023/2024) Evaluating large language models in theory of mind tasks, PNAS
finding: 40 bespoke false-belief tasks, each with 3 true-belief controls and reversed versions; a task counts only if all 8 scenarios pass. Older models solved none; newer solved some.
numbers: davinci-003 and ChatGPT-3.5-turbo solved 20%; ChatGPT-4 solved 75%. Paper states this matches 6-year-old children from earlier studies. Readout is next-word probability, for example popcorn/chocolate bag and cat in box/basket.
limits: Text only, one lab, GPT family. Contradicted by trivial-alteration studies (Ullman, Shapira). Success may use word-order or frequency cues.
agent_relevance: Strong headline that dissolves under small perturbation. Never accept a pass on the standard form alone (G3).

source: Ullman (2023) Large language models fail on trivial alterations to theory-of-mind tasks
finding: Small changes that keep the ToM logic (transparent bag, protagonist who can see inside, moved cat) flip GPT-3.5 answers. Zero-hypothesis should be skeptical; failures outweigh average success.
numbers: Kosinski original: content prompt P(popcorn)=100%, first belief prompt P(chocolate)=99%. In altered variants where the protagonist could see the contents, belief prompts still printed values near 87% to 98% for the wrong answer (values listed in the paper).
limits: GPT-3.5 only; a few hand-built items; no human control sample. Later models not tested here.
agent_relevance: Same logic as Povinelli-style controls: one version proves little. Add perturbed variants to every social-cognition probe.

source: Shapira et al. (2023) Clever Hans or Neural Theory of Mind? Stress testing social reasoning in LLMs
finding: Six ToM tasks on many LLMs. Abilities appear on easy items but break under adversarial variants. Authors tie this to Clever Hans.
numbers: GPT-4: 97% on original false-belief items, but 0% on 'transparent access' and 'inon' adversarial categories; other-person category 68.8% (93.8% by davinci-002). FauxPas-EAI best model 27%, below a most-frequent-class baseline. One subset total 79%, 'others' 74.5%.
limits: Mostly GPT family and Flan-T5. Probing method changes accuracy (7% gap between MC and CoT probing for GPT-4 on SIQA).
agent_relevance: Confirms shallow-cue reliance. Use adversarial controls and report the worst case, not the mean.

source: Strachan et al. (2024) Testing theory of mind in large language models and humans, Nat Hum Behav
finding: Battery (false belief, irony, faux pas, hinting, strange stories) given to GPT-4, GPT-3.5, LLaMA2-70B and 1,907 humans. GPT-4 matched or beat humans on false belief, indirect requests and misdirection; weak on faux pas.
numbers: 15 chats per model per test; about 50 humans per test, 1,907 overall. False belief at ceiling for humans and LLMs (novel items near perfect; 5 of 51 humans made one error). Faux pas: GPT poor, LLaMA2-70B above humans, but belief-likelihood tests suggest LLaMA2's edge is a bias to attribute ignorance and GPT's failure is hyperconservatism.
limits: Text only. Authors note ceiling false-belief performance may rest on lower-level explanations. Novel items used to avoid training-data copying.
agent_relevance: A matched human/LLM protocol with novel items and likelihood probes separates a real gap from a response-bias artefact. Reuse the design.

source: Penn & Povinelli (2007) On the lack of evidence that non-human animals possess anything remotely resembling a 'theory of mind', Phil Trans R Soc B
finding: (From memory) Argues animal evidence is explained by behaviour-reading and does not need representation of unobservable mental states.
numbers: None recorded.
limits: Not opened. Main sceptical review beside Emery & Clayton 2004.
agent_relevance: Behaviour-reading rules can mimic mindreading; keep rules simple until a perturbation fails.

source: Emery & Clayton (2004) The mentality of crows: convergent evolution of intelligence in corvids and apes, Science 306:1903
finding: (From memory, matches SUBFIELDS.md) Proposes corvids and apes share a tool kit of causal reasoning, flexibility, imagination and prospection through convergent evolution.
numbers: None recorded.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Convergent solutions to social problems suggest function matters more than substrate.

source: Call & Tomasello (2008) Does the chimpanzee have a theory of mind? 30 years later, Trends Cogn Sci 12:187
finding: (From memory) Concludes chimpanzees understand goals, perception and knowledge, with no good false-belief evidence at that date. Not opened.
numbers: None recorded.
limits: Not opened; reference seen in the Krupenye 2016 and Heyes 2015 chains.
agent_relevance: Sets the 2008 baseline that Krupenye 2016 then moved.

source: Kano et al. (2017) Eye tracking uncovered great apes' ability to anticipate false beliefs, Commun Integr Biol (PMC5398232)
finding: Authors' own mini-review of the eye-tracking false-belief study and why apes may succeed on implicit but not explicit tasks.
numbers: Page text fetched (about 40k characters); no new numbers used here.
limits: Authors' own account, not independent.
agent_relevance: Two systems appear: implicit belief tracking and explicit choice. The same split recurs in the LLM debate.

source: Link: 05_prospection_and_mental_time_travel (same A18 folder)
finding: Pointer only. Emery & Clayton caching also bears on prospection and episodic-like memory, covered there. Not repeated here.
numbers: None.
